paragraphs: ALINE tackles a paired problem: deciding what data to collect next and quickly updating an inference after receiving it. These decisions are closely connected because the usefulness of a measurement depends on what the system is trying to learn. The paper combines Bayesian inference and active data acquisition in one trained framework.

Its transformer is trained with reinforcement learning. The reward comes from information gain estimated by its own inference component, so the mechanism that interprets observations also helps guide future queries. This connects data selection directly to the system’s evolving predictions. ALINE can also focus acquisition on selected model parameters or particular prediction tasks, rather than treating every unknown as equally important.

The authors evaluate the framework on regression active learning, Bayesian experimental design benchmarks, and a psychometric model with targeted parameters. They report fast, accurate inference alongside efficient selection of informative observations. These findings support the value of jointly learning how to ask questions and how to use their answers, including when the learning objective concerns only part of a model.
neurips-2025-aline-joint-amortization-fo.tldr: ALINE jointly learns Bayesian inference and informative data selection, with the ability to target specific parameters or prediction tasks.

paragraphs: BurstDeflicker addresses dark brightness bands that appear when a rolling shutter camera captures lighting whose intensity changes over time. Because different image rows are exposed at different moments, a short exposure can record uneven illumination. These artifacts affect image quality and can also interfere with object detection and tracking.

The paper builds a benchmark through three complementary acquisition strategies. A Retinex-based synthesis pipeline creates controllable flicker patterns, varying properties such as intensity, affected area, and frequency. A collection of 4,000 real flicker images adds examples of how the phenomenon behaves across actual scenes. Together, synthetic control and real observations provide different kinds of training evidence.

The third strategy uses a green screen to introduce motion into image pairs while retaining real flicker degradation. This addresses the difficulty of repeating a dynamic scene to obtain paired observations. Experiments support the dataset’s effectiveness for flicker removal. The contribution is a way to combine diverse controlled artifacts, realistic lighting behavior, and moving content within a scalable benchmark.
neurips-2025-burstdeflicker-a-benchmark-.tldr: BurstDeflicker combines synthetic flicker, real captures, and green-screen motion to support realistic flicker-removal research.

paragraphs: CineTechBench examines whether AI systems can understand and reproduce the visual techniques used in filmmaking. Recognizing what appears in a scene does not by itself assess how camera position, movement, or lighting shapes its presentation. The paper creates an expert-annotated benchmark specifically for these cinematographic choices.

Experienced cinematographers manually label more than 600 movie images and 120 clips. The annotations cover shot scale, shot angle, composition, camera movement, lighting, color, and focal length. For understanding, the benchmark uses questions, answers, and annotated descriptions to assess how well multimodal language models interpret and explain these techniques.

The generation evaluation asks video models to reconstruct cinematic camera movements from conditions such as text prompts or keyframes. The authors evaluate more than 15 multimodal language models and more than five video generation models. Their results identify limitations in current systems and suggest directions for further work. By evaluating both interpretation and production, the benchmark connects cinematic knowledge with the ability to carry out a specified visual technique.
neurips-2025-cinetechbench-a-benchmark-f.tldr: CineTechBench uses expert film annotations to evaluate AI understanding of cinematography and generation of cinematic camera movements.

paragraphs: This paper asks which stimuli and features account for the information carried by sensory neurons. Mutual information measures the overall amount, but dividing that total among individual stimuli is ambiguous: many different assignments can have the same average. Fisher information describes sensitivity to tiny changes, but does not provide the required decomposition of total information.

The authors propose axioms for an interpretable attribution: nonnegative contributions, additivity across repeated measurements, locality, and insensitivity to irrelevant features. Locality means that changing a neuron’s response to one stimulus should not change the information assigned to a distant stimulus. They show that existing decompositions violate at least one proposed requirement and introduce a decomposition satisfying all of them.

The new measure captures sensitivity to both tiny and finite changes and can assign information to individual features, including image pixels. Diffusion models make its computation tractable for high-dimensional stimuli and large neural populations. Demonstrations with a model of visual neurons reveal information patterns missed by standard methods, including Fisher information. Applications to higher sensory areas and artificial networks are presented as future possibilities.
neurips-2025-decomposing-stimulus-specif.tldr: The paper introduces an axiom-based decomposition of neural information into stimulus and feature contributions, made tractable through diffusion models.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether fairness requirements imposed on individual machine-learning classifiers also produce fair outcomes across competing firms. The distinction matters because people experience the combined effects of multiple decision makers. A fairness assessment of one classifier therefore addresses a different question from an assessment of the surrounding ecosystem.

The authors introduce a model of fairness under competition and analyze how ecosystem outcomes depend on relationships between classifiers. Their results quantify fairness losses under various conditions involving classifier correlation and overlap in the data they use. This makes the interaction among firms part of the fairness analysis, rather than evaluating each decision system independently.

The theoretical results show that individually fair classifiers can collectively produce unfair outcomes. They also show that improving an algorithm’s individual fairness can, under the studied conditions, reduce overall ecosystem fairness. Supporting experiments accompany the analysis. The conclusion is conditional rather than a claim that fairness adjustments always backfire: local fairness improvements do not by themselves establish that the combined system has become fairer.
neurips-2025-fairness-under-competition-.tldr: Individually fair classifiers can produce unfair outcomes across competing firms, and local fairness improvements can sometimes worsen ecosystem fairness.

paragraphs: FALCON automates analog circuit design from requested performance specifications. This involves choosing a circuit structure, determining its parameters, and accounting for layout feasibility. The framework connects these stages so that parameter selection considers physical design constraints alongside predicted electrical performance.

A classifier guided by human design heuristics first selects a topology. An edge-centric graph neural network then predicts performance from the circuit’s structure and parameters. The system uses gradients through this learned forward model to infer suitable parameter values. A differentiable layout cost incorporates analytical descriptions of parasitic and frequency-dependent effects, while design rules constrain the optimization.

The authors train and evaluate FALCON using one million simulated analog millimeter-wave circuits spanning 20 expert-designed topologies. They report topology inference accuracy above 99%, relative performance prediction error below 10%, and layout-aware design taking under one second per instance. These results support the framework’s usefulness within the evaluated design setting. Its central contribution is bringing topology selection, learned performance prediction, and layout-constrained parameter inference into one automated process.
neurips-2025-falcon-an-ml-framework-for-.tldr: FALCON combines topology selection, graph-based performance prediction, and layout-constrained optimization to automate analog circuit design.

paragraphs: The paper develops a flexible family of probability distributions for black-box variational inference, where a tractable distribution approximates a target density. Each approximation multiplies together weighted experts based on multivariate t-distributions. This family can represent asymmetry, heavy tails, and multiple modes, but using it requires a practical way to obtain samples.

The authors apply a Feynman identity to rewrite the product as a latent-variable model with auxiliary Dirichlet variables. This representation enables weighted sampling from the product of experts. The identity supplies a computational route for using an expressive distribution family that would otherwise be difficult to handle in the inference procedure.

For a given collection of experts, the method iteratively adjusts their exponents by matching the scores of the approximation and target density. Each update minimizes a regularized Fisher divergence through a convex quadratic program. Under general conditions, the authors prove exponential convergence to a near-optimal weighting. They also evaluate synthetic and real-world targets. The guarantee concerns the weighting of the supplied experts, rather than exact recovery of every possible target distribution.
neurips-2025-fisher-meets-feynman-score-.tldr: A Feynman identity enables sampling from expressive products of t-distribution experts, whose weights are optimized through score matching.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models can grow to very large parameter counts while activating only part of the model, avoiding a proportional increase in computation. Training them across GPUs still requires coordinating computation and communication. FlowMoE addresses that coordination by scheduling a broader set of training operations together.

The paper identifies a gap in earlier scheduling approaches: they concentrate mainly on expert computation and all-to-all communication within the MoE layer. FlowMoE builds a unified pipeline that also includes multi-head attention computation and gating. Bringing these operations into the same schedule lets the framework coordinate work that earlier approaches largely left outside their scheduling scope.

FlowMoE also introduces a priority scheduling mechanism based on tensor chunks. This mechanism overlaps all-reduce communication with computing tasks, allowing communication and computation to proceed concurrently. The authors implement the combined approach as an adaptive, general framework built on PyTorch.

The reported evaluation covers 675 typical MoE layers and four real-world MoE models on two GPU clusters. Compared with state-of-the-art MoE training frameworks, FlowMoE reduces training time by 14%–57%, energy consumption by 10%–39%, and memory usage by 7%–32%. These measured improvements support the value of coordinating multiple operation types, with benefits spanning speed, energy, and memory in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-flowmoe-a-scalable-pipeline.tldr: FlowMoE coordinates more computation and communication tasks in distributed Mixture-of-Experts training, reducing training time, energy consumption, and memory usage in its reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper develops moderation that can judge a language model’s response while it is still being generated. Waiting for the complete response adds latency, but applying a conventional full-response moderator to unfinished text creates a mismatch between training and use. The authors address that mismatch with data and training designed for partial outputs.

They introduce FineHarm, containing 29,000 prompt-response pairs with token-level annotations. Their Streaming Content Monitor learns from both labels for entire responses and labels attached to individual tokens. This dual supervision supports judgments as the output stream arrives, allowing harmful generation to be stopped before the response is complete.

In the reported experiments, the monitor achieves a macro F1 score above 0.95, comparable to full-response detection, while seeing only the first 18% of response tokens on average. That is an average observation requirement, not a fixed stopping point for every response. The monitor can also supply pseudo-labels for safety alignment; the authors report a higher harmlessness score than DPO when using it in that role.
neurips-2025-from-judgment-to-interferen.tldr: Token-level supervision lets a streaming moderator detect harmful responses early with reported accuracy comparable to full-response moderation.

paragraphs: Generalized Contrastive Learning addresses retrieval across different combinations of images and text. Models that perform well when matching one modality to another can struggle when a retrieved item contains both, such as a page with an image and accompanying text. The goal is a shared retrieval model that handles these varied combinations.

One existing approach creates specially composed image-text triplets for particular retrieval tasks. The abstract identifies two problems with that approach: substantial curation effort and poor generalization to unseen modality combinations. GCL instead changes the training loss, enforcing contrastive learning across all modalities within each mini-batch of existing image-caption pairs.

This training objective teaches a unified representation space without requiring a newly curated collection of composed examples. The authors apply GCL to existing retrieval models, including VISTA, CLIP, and TinyCLIP, and report consistent improvements on M-BEIR, MMEB, and CoVR. The results support changing how available paired data is used to improve multimodal retrieval, with the contribution concentrated in the learning objective rather than in constructing another specialized dataset.
neurips-2025-generalized-contrastive-lea.tldr: GCL improves retrieval across image-text combinations by changing contrastive training on existing image-caption data.

paragraphs: GenSpace evaluates whether image generators follow instructions about three-dimensional scene structure. A picture can look attractive and broadly match a prompt while placing objects incorrectly or failing to respect specified relationships and measurements. The benchmark focuses on these spatial requirements in generation from text or image prompts.

The authors also address how to measure such errors. They find that evaluations using general vision-language models frequently miss detailed spatial mistakes. Their specialized pipeline combines multiple visual foundation models to reconstruct scene geometry in three dimensions, then uses that reconstruction to assess spatial faithfulness. They report that the resulting metric is more accurate and better aligned with human judgment.

The evaluation identifies three recurring weaknesses: understanding object perspective, translating between viewer-centered and scene-centered spatial descriptions, and following metric measurements. Current generators can produce appealing images and follow general instructions while still struggling with these details. GenSpace therefore separates visual quality from compliance with spatial constraints and provides a targeted way to examine where that compliance breaks down.
neurips-2025-genspace-benchmarking-spati.tldr: GenSpace evaluates 3D spatial faithfulness in generated images using reconstructed scene geometry and identifies persistent spatial weaknesses.

paragraphs: MESS+ chooses which language model should handle each incoming request while balancing operating cost against service-quality requirements. A collection of available models offers many choices, but users generally care about response quality rather than model selection. The paper frames this decision around service level agreements that specify minimum acceptable service.

The algorithm learns each model’s probability of satisfying requests as users interact with the system. It combines those predictions with virtual queues and solves an optimization problem for each request. This makes routing responsive to learned satisfaction probabilities while incorporating the service constraints into the selection process.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of cost optimality and constraint satisfaction, including rigorous guarantees for SLA compliance. Across the evaluated language-model benchmarks, MESS+ achieves average cost savings of twofold relative to existing routing methods. The contribution combines online learning about request satisfaction with constrained routing decisions. The reported savings concern the benchmark comparison; the service guarantees concern the algorithm’s analyzed constraints, rather than a promise that every individual answer is correct.
neurips-2025-mess-dynamically-learned-in.tldr: MESS+ learns model satisfaction probabilities online and routes requests to reduce cost while providing analyzed service-level guarantees.

paragraphs: MVU-Eval tests how well multimodal language models understand information spread across multiple videos. Existing evaluations centered on single videos leave this capability insufficiently examined. Applications such as sports analysis across camera angles and synthesis of multiple sensors require models to combine evidence across video inputs.

The benchmark contains 1,824 curated question-answer pairs spanning 4,959 videos from varied domains. It assesses eight competencies, covering both basic perception and more demanding reasoning. The authors align these abilities with practical uses, including cross-angle sports analysis and multi-sensor interpretation in autonomous systems. This gives the evaluation a broader target than recognizing content within an isolated clip.

Tests of leading open-source and closed-source models reveal substantial differences in performance and limitations in multi-video understanding. The findings show that this setting exposes capabilities that need direct evaluation rather than being inferred from single-video results. The paper’s main contribution is a structured benchmark for measuring those abilities and comparing systems; it does not introduce a model that resolves the observed weaknesses.
neurips-2025-mvu-eval-towards-multi-vide.tldr: MVU-Eval tests eight multi-video understanding competencies and reveals substantial performance gaps among current multimodal language models.

paragraphs: NeuSA addresses difficulties that standard physics-informed neural networks encounter when solving complex initial value problems. Networks based on multilayer perceptrons can fail to converge, violate the time-directed structure of the problem, and favor low-frequency components. The paper changes the architecture to reflect both spectral structure and causal evolution.

The method learns a projection of a partial differential equation onto a spectral basis. This produces a finite-dimensional description of the dynamics, which an adapted Neural ODE then integrates. The spectral representation supplies high-frequency components, while the Neural ODE provides a causal structure for advancing the solution. An initialization scheme based on classical methods starts training near the target solution.

The framework is designed for linear and nonlinear equations with variable coefficients. On canonical linear and nonlinear wave-equation benchmarks, the authors report faster convergence, better temporal consistency, and higher predictive accuracy than the compared architectures. These findings support combining classical numerical structure with learned components so that the representation and time evolution directly address the stated failure modes.
neurips-2025-neuro-spectral-architecture.tldr: NeuSA combines learned spectral representations with Neural ODE integration to improve convergence, causality, and accuracy in physics-informed networks.

paragraphs: This paper extends Direct Preference Optimization so that a comparison can explicitly declare two responses tied. Standard preference modeling emphasizes a winner and loser, while real comparisons can contain no clear preference. The authors derive two DPO variants using the Rao–Kupper and Davidson extensions of the Bradley–Terry model, both of which assign probability to ties.

In translation and summarization experiments, the variants can incorporate labeled ties without the task-performance degradation observed when the same tied pairs are given to ordinary DPO. The authors also find that including ties keeps the learned policy closer to its reference policy, as measured by KL divergence. This regularization effect appears even with the original DPO formulation.

The paper explains that effect theoretically using ideal DPO policy theory and reports improvements over DPO in translation and mathematical reasoning. Together, the results suggest that ties can carry useful training information. The supported conclusion is that retaining them can help when modeled appropriately, rather than that adding ties necessarily improves every preference-optimization task.
neurips-2025-on-extending-direct-prefere.tldr: Two tie-aware DPO variants make equal-preference comparisons usable and show benefits for regularization and several evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies fair division of a divisible resource when agents value its parts differently. It introduces two fairness hierarchies that consider the combined value assigned to groups of agents. For each observer, groups containing that observer receive a minimum-value guarantee, while groups excluding them face a maximum-value bound, offering protection against coalition formation.

Both hierarchies reduce to proportionality at level one. Every envy-free allocation satisfies every level of the first hierarchy. The second has a more intricate relationship with envy-freeness: intermediate levels can be incomparable, while levels at least half the number of agents, rounded up, imply envy-freeness. Its final level equals super envy-freeness, bounding each other agent’s piece by one nth of the total value.

The computational distinction is sharp in the Robertson–Webb query model. The strongest first-hierarchy requirement can be achieved with O(n⁴) queries, while even its second level requires Ω(n²). For the second hierarchy, already level two cannot be computed with a query bound depending only on n. These results show how related forms of group protection can have dramatically different computational demands.
neurips-2025-on-hierarchies-of-fairness-.tldr: Two coalition-aware fairness hierarchies connect classic cake-cutting notions while revealing sharply different query-complexity boundaries.

paragraphs: GenComm helps agents with different sensors and perception models share useful information. Their internal representations can differ enough that exchanging features creates a domain gap. The paper also identifies a practical problem with adaptation: retraining core modules can disturb established semantic consistency and make adding collaborators computationally expensive.

The method sends extracted spatial messages in place of intermediate features. A Deformable Message Extractor prepares each collaborator’s spatial information, and a conditional diffusion model generates features compatible with the receiving agent’s semantic space. A Channel Enhancer refines these generated features before fusion. Lightweight numerical alignment supports integration of new agents without modifying the original network.

Evaluations on OPV2V-H, DAIR-V2X, and V2X-Real show improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report an 81% reduction in both computational cost and parameter count when adding agents. The approach’s central idea is to preserve shared spatial content while generating the representation needed by the receiver, addressing both perception quality and the cost of expanding a heterogeneous collaboration.
neurips-2025-pragmatic-heterogeneous-col.tldr: GenComm turns shared spatial messages into receiver-compatible features, improving heterogeneous collaboration while reducing the cost of adding agents.

paragraphs: This paper studies online pricing algorithms that remain consistent despite variation in their input data. Such replicability matters for transparency in economic decisions: the analysis asks how to obtain stable algorithmic behavior while retaining strong pricing performance. The authors investigate this requirement for prophet inequalities and extend their findings to delegation.

They construct a replicable, nearly optimal pricing strategy whose sample complexity is polynomial in log-star of the size of the distribution ground set. Log-star is an iterated logarithm, making this a very slowly growing dependence on the ground-set size. A lower bound shows that dependence on this iterated-logarithm quantity is necessary, so it cannot simply be eliminated.

The proof development also produces an algorithm for a variant of the heavy hitter problem. Its dependence on the inverse heavy hitter parameter is nearly linear, improving on an existing cubic dependence. The contribution therefore includes both pricing guarantees and a separate technical improvement. The pricing result establishes near-optimality together with replicability, rather than treating consistency as an informal property of repeated runs.
neurips-2025-replicable-online-pricing-0.tldr: The paper develops nearly optimal replicable pricing with iterated-logarithmic sample dependence and proves that this dependence is necessary.

paragraphs: RetrievalAttention reduces the memory and decoding costs of language models working with long contexts. Storing the context’s key and value vectors consumes substantial GPU memory, while attention over those vectors slows generation. The method builds indexes for fixed contexts and maintains them in CPU memory, retrieving relevant vectors during decoding.

The approach integrates approximate nearest-neighbor search into attention computation without additional model training. Ordinary search indexes are not sufficient in the authors’ analysis because attention queries and keys have an out-of-distribution relationship. RetrievalAttention uses an attention-aware index designed to address that mismatch and make selective access effective.

The evaluation reports accuracy close to full attention while accessing only 1–3% of the data. It also demonstrates an eight-billion-parameter model processing a 128,000-token context on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with decoding at 0.107 seconds per token. The result shows how CPU-resident indexing and selective attention access can support long contexts on constrained GPU memory, while the accuracy claim remains approximate rather than identical to full attention.
neurips-2025-retrievalattention-accelera.tldr: RetrievalAttention uses CPU-resident, attention-aware vector indexes to accelerate long-context decoding with accuracy close to full attention.

paragraphs: SageAttention3 investigates lower-precision attention for both inference and training. Attention’s quadratic time complexity makes its efficiency consequential as workloads grow. The paper separates two contributions: an FP4 implementation that uses specialized Blackwell GPU hardware and an eight-bit attention method designed for training.

For inference, the FP4 implementation reaches 1,038 TOPS on an RTX 5090, reported as five times the speed of the fastest FlashAttention implementation on that GPU. Experiments show that it can accelerate inference across various models through plug-and-play integration. The fivefold result describes attention implementation performance on the stated hardware, rather than a fivefold end-to-end speedup for every model.

For training, the authors design eight-bit attention for both forward and backward propagation. Their experiments report no performance loss in fine-tuning tasks, but slower convergence during pretraining. This distinction is central to the findings: successful low-bit inference does not settle how the same broad efficiency strategy behaves during learning. The training results support fine-tuning use in the tested settings while identifying a convergence issue for pretraining.
neurips-2025-sageattention3-microscaling.tldr: SageAttention3 accelerates inference with FP4 attention and finds eight-bit attention preserves fine-tuning performance but slows pretraining convergence.

paragraphs: SCAN improves the synthetic supervision used to train process reward models, which evaluate individual reasoning steps. Human step annotations are costly, while Monte Carlo estimates offer a scalable alternative with substantial noise. The authors find that annotation models can both underestimate and overestimate whether a step is correct.

The framework combines self-denoising data synthesis with a learning strategy designed to tolerate noisy labels. This addresses annotation quality and the reward model’s ability to learn from imperfect supervision together. The authors report that even a 1.5-billion-parameter annotation model can produce high-quality labels through self-denoising, supporting superior reward-model performance at only 6% of the inference cost of vanilla Monte Carlo estimation.

On ProcessBench, the robust learning strategy raises F1 from 19.9 to 59.1, an increase of 39.2 points. Models trained on a compact synthetic dataset outperform strong baselines, including models trained on large human-annotated datasets such as PRM800K. Performance also improves as synthetic data increases. These findings support denoising and noise-tolerant learning as complementary routes to more scalable step-level reward supervision.
neurips-2025-scan-self-denoising-monte-c.tldr: SCAN combines self-denoising annotations with noise-tolerant learning to improve process reward models at substantially lower annotation cost.

paragraphs: SubSpec accelerates language models whose parameters cannot all fit in GPU memory. Offloading preserves model quality but slows generation because weights must be transferred during computation. Speculative decoding can reduce this overhead by proposing several tokens with a faster draft model and checking them together with the target model.

The method constructs its draft directly from the target model without additional training. It creates low-bit substitute layers for the offloaded portions, while sharing the layers already on the GPU and the key-value cache. This design reduces extra memory requirements and keeps the draft closely aligned with the target, helping more proposed tokens pass verification.

The authors describe SubSpec as lossless and report high average token acceptance lengths. For Qwen2.5 7B on MT-Bench under an 8 GB VRAM limit, they report a 9.1-fold speedup. For Qwen2.5 32B under a 24 GB limit, the average speedup is 12.5-fold across generation benchmarks. These results connect better draft alignment with fewer expensive offloaded forward passes in the evaluated deployment settings.
neurips-2025-speculate-deep-and-accurate.tldr: SubSpec creates a training-free draft from quantized substitutes and shared target-model components to accelerate offloaded inference without quality loss.

paragraphs: TokMan optimizes lithography masks while preserving the axis-aligned geometry used in semiconductor manufacturing. Optical distortions can make the printed wafer differ from its intended layout, so inverse lithography adjusts the mask to compensate. Learning-based approaches can achieve good simulated printing fidelity yet generate curved shapes that violate Manhattan geometry constraints.

The paper treats mask optimization as a discrete sequence-modeling problem built around geometric structure. A Diffusion Transformer uses discrete geometric primitives and dependencies between polygon elements to denoise Manhattan-aligned point sequences. This representation makes binary, manufacturable mask geometry part of the optimization approach, rather than relying only on a continuous pixel grid.

Training uses self-supervised lithographic feedback from a differentiable simulator, followed by inverse-lithography post-processing. On a large-scale integrated-circuit layout dataset, the authors report state-of-the-art fidelity, runtime efficiency, and strict manufacturing compliance. The significance is the joint treatment of optical compensation and geometric validity: the optimized output must both print the intended pattern accurately and satisfy the manufacturing structure required of the mask.
neurips-2025-tokman-tokenize-manhattan-m.tldr: TokMan models lithography masks as discrete geometric sequences to improve printing fidelity while preserving Manhattan manufacturing constraints.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why message passing can work on graphs where connected nodes differ. Standard graph neural networks fit naturally with homophily, the assumption that neighbors are similar. Yet methods for heterophilic graphs often still succeed by exchanging information between neighbors, motivating a closer explanation from the model’s perspective.

The authors connect how well nodes can be distinguished with a compatibility matrix and introduce Compatibility Matrix Discriminability. Their analysis suggests that successful message passing in heterophilic networks may be explained by increases in this quantity. This provides a proposed model-level account of the phenomenon, extending beyond explanations centered only on properties of the input data.

Using that connection, they develop CMGNN to improve the compatibility matrix and node embeddings explicitly while mitigating sparsity and noise. Those two issues make the matrix difficult to use effectively. Evaluation across 13 datasets and against 20 established baselines favors CMGNN. The contribution therefore links an explanatory measure with an architecture designed around it, while retaining the qualified claim about why message passing succeeds.
neurips-2025-understanding-and-enhancing.tldr: CMGNN uses compatibility-matrix discriminability to explain and improve message passing on graphs with dissimilar neighbors.

paragraphs: This paper improves multiview 3D human pose estimation without requiring camera calibration. Multiple views provide complementary evidence, but learning their interactions entirely through flexible continuous representations can allow noisy inputs to contaminate other views. The resulting errors can propagate and accumulate in the final pose estimate.

The authors introduce UniCodebook, a compact discrete representation that supplies a noise-resilient prior alongside continuous pose features. The aim is to retain the continuous model’s ability to regress poses while adding the robustness offered by a constrained discrete representation. A Discrete-Continuous Spatial Attention mechanism coordinates the two, preserving their attributes and encouraging them to contribute complementary information.

Experiments on three representative datasets show the approach outperforming both calibration-dependent and calibration-free methods, with state-of-the-art performance reported. The contribution addresses a specific weakness of unrestricted learned view interactions: their susceptibility to noise spreading across views. Combining discrete priors with continuous features provides a way to constrain those interactions while preserving the flexibility needed for pose estimation.
neurips-2025-unified-2d-3d-discrete-prio.tldr: UniCodebook combines discrete pose priors with continuous features to improve noise robustness in calibration-free multiview 3D pose estimation.
